source_text: Munus similaginis cum oleo et ture — laus et oratio. Sacerdos memoriale incendit. Qui non potest pecudem, offert farinam: misericordia gradus pauperum novit.
thought_title: The poor person's offering of fine flour
orientation: Origen is explaining the graduated offerings in Leviticus, now turning to the offering of fine flour with oil and frankincense as the sacrifice of the poor.
pass_a_gloss: Gift [of] fine flour with oil and frankincense — praise and prayer. [The] priest [the] memorial burns. [He] who not is able [a] beast, offers flour: [the] mercy [of] steps [of the] poor knows.

choices.why: Keeps munus as gift per the brief's sense of offering, and similago as fine flour to distinguish from ordinary farina.
Memoriale is a technical cultic term for the portion burned as a reminder before God; rendering as memorial portion preserves the ritual sense.

choices.english: mercy knows the steps of the poor
choices.why: Gradus means steps or degrees; the phrase means mercy recognizes the graduated levels of what the poor can offer. Kept literal to preserve the metaphor.
rejected: mercy understands the ranks of the poor
compassion knows the stages of poverty

choices.why: Origen interprets the flour, oil, and frankincense spiritually as praise and prayer; the dash in the source marks this as an interpretive gloss, kept as such.

bible_refs.note: munus similaginis cum oleo et ture; sacerdos memoriale incendit
qui non potest pecudem, offert farinam

pass_b_english: A gift of fine flour with oil and frankincense means praise and prayer. The priest burns the memorial portion. The one who cannot offer an animal offers flour: mercy acknowledges the degrees of poverty.

problems.quote: mercy knows the steps of the poor
problems.why: Gradus means 'degrees/levels/ranks', not 'steps' as footsteps; novit means 'knows/recognizes/acknowledges'. The sense is that mercy acknowledges or makes allowance for the varying degrees/conditions of poverty, not that mercy literally knows footsteps.
problems.fix: mercy acknowledges the degrees of poverty
problems.ruling: Gradus means 'degrees/levels'; 'steps of the poor' misleads, losing sense that mercy accounts for varying degrees of poverty.

edits.old: mercy knows the steps of the poor
edits.new: mercy acknowledges the degrees of poverty

fixed: Changed 'mercy knows the steps of the poor' to 'mercy acknowledges the degrees of poverty': gradus here means degrees/levels/ranks, and novit means acknowledges/recognizes, so the English misstated the source.

last_rejected.quote: mercy acknowledges the degrees of poverty
last_rejected.why: Misericordia is mercy, but novit here means 'knows' not 'acknowledges'; gradus pauperum means 'steps/degrees of the poor'—the poor's steps are known to mercy, i.e., God mercifully recognizes different poverty levels. English inverts subject and object, making mercy the active knower/acknowledger rather than the poor's steps being known to mercy.
last_rejected.fix: mercy knows the steps of the poor
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'misericordia gradus pauperum novit' has misericordia as subject; English correctly renders it. 'Acknowledges' is within novit's range.
